extracted.intended_audience: Canadian researchers, science policymakers, and the general public interested in research funding and gender equity
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how different peer-review criteria and processes used by grant agencies (applicant-focused vs project-focused, blinded review, training) affect gender disparities in research funding outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review focus: applicant versus science
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers evaluate the scientist (the applicant) versus the proposed project (the science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that when reviewers are told to focus on evaluating the scientists it "significantly amplifies success rates for men." In contrast, focusing review on the proposed project produced similar success rates for male and female applicants (Project Grants: 13.5% men vs 12% women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project Grant Program criterion — evaluate ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Project Grant Program evaluates "ideas with the greatest potential," i.e., focuses on the proposed project rather than the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this program men and women performed similarly (13.5% success for men vs 12% for women), suggesting project-focused review reduces observed gender gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation Grant Program criterion — evaluate research leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundation Grant Program evaluates "research leaders," i.e., places emphasis on the applicant's track record and leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this program men had higher success (13.9% men vs 9.2% women). The disparity was especially large in public health (14.1% men vs 6.7% women), indicating applicant-focused criteria can exacerbate gender gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for covariates (age and field of study) in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses of funding outcomes should account for applicant age and field of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lancet analysis of nearly 24,000 CIHR applications "took applicants' age and field of study into account," and still found robust evidence of gender differences tied to review focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistical evidence to reveal bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on large-scale statistical analysis rather than individual anecdotes to detect systemic bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study analyzed almost 24,000 applications and used comparative success rates across programs to show that bias emerges when review emphasizes the applicant; commentary notes you "can really only see the bias in the statistics."

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded (anonymous) review to reduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing applicant identity during review to reduce unintended bias against certain groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts in the article (e.g., Jennifer Raymond) support a 'blinded' grant application process; the Toronto Symphony Orchestra's blind auditions are cited as an example where hiding identities transformed gender balance in hiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious-bias training for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide training to reviewers to mitigate implicit biases affecting peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CIHR developed an online course called 'Unconscious Bias in Peer Review' as a step toward eliminating 'systemic biases against any individual or group.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor cumulative (career-stage) effects of funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how early-career funding decisions compound over time to affect publications, lab recruitment, and future funding opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that "getting funding can lead to more publications" and further opportunities, so small early advantages can accumulate and stall the careers of disadvantaged groups; consequently, review criteria should be assessed for long-term career impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare applicant pool composition to award rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess equity by comparing proportions of applicants by gender (or other group) to proportions of successful awardees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes overall men submitted twice as many applications as women, and in public health women outnumbered men but received a smaller share of Foundation grants — a diagnostic metric for bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize discipline-specific disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how gender gaps vary across fields (e.g., public health versus other disciplines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disparity was most striking in public health, where female applicants outnumber male applicants but men were twice as likely to win Foundation grants (14.1% vs 6.7%), indicating field-specific dynamics matter when evaluating review criteria.
